clinicalPearls: An autoimmune inflammatory disorder of the pituitary that classically affects women in late pregnancy or the postpartum period
Increasingly recognised as an immune-related adverse effect of checkpoint-inhibitor cancer therapy
Headache and visual disturbance from an enlarging, inflamed gland can mimic a pituitary adenoma
Hormone loss often occurs in a characteristic sequence, with corticotroph and thyrotroph function frequently affected early
Involvement of the posterior pituitary or stalk can cause diabetes insipidus, which is unusual in adenomas and a useful discriminating clue
Imaging typically shows symmetrical pituitary enlargement with stalk thickening and avid, homogeneous enhancement
Corticotroph deficiency must be identified and treated with hormone replacement before any thyroid hormone is started
The condition may be self-limiting, and glucocorticoid therapy or drug withdrawal is used depending on the underlying trigger
reference.pathophysiology: Lymphocytic hypophysitis is characterised by immune-mediated infiltration of the pituitary gland by lymphocytes and plasma cells, producing inflammation, gland enlargement and progressive destruction of hormone-secreting cells. The classic form has a strong association with the peripartum state and other autoimmune conditions, suggesting a breakdown in immune tolerance to pituitary antigens. Checkpoint-inhibitor therapy can trigger a similar inflammatory hypophysitis by unleashing autoreactive immunity. Inflammation may involve the anterior lobe, the stalk and the posterior lobe, accounting for the variable pattern of anterior hormone deficiencies and, in some cases, diabetes insipidus, with eventual fibrosis and atrophy.
additionalDifferentials: Langerhans cell histiocytosis involving the pituitary
additionalInvestigations: Magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary and stalk
Full anterior pituitary hormone profile including cortisol assessment
Assessment for diabetes insipidus with paired plasma and urine osmolality
Prolactin measurement, which may be mildly elevated or reduced
Review of any recent checkpoint-inhibitor or other immunotherapy exposure
redFlags: Rapid visual deterioration from chiasmal compression
New diabetes insipidus indicating posterior or stalk involvement
Severe headache with a rapidly enlarging sellar mass
reference.prognosis: Many cases stabilise or partially recover, particularly with treatment of the trigger, but some hormone deficits, especially corticotroph loss, are permanent and require lifelong replacement; checkpoint-inhibitor-related corticotroph deficiency is often irreversible.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the inflamed gland as a pituitary adenoma and proceeding to unnecessary surgery
Starting thyroid hormone before replacing cortisol and precipitating an adrenal crisis
Overlooking diabetes insipidus as a distinguishing feature
Failing to consider checkpoint-inhibitor therapy as a cause in cancer patients
Assuming full recovery of pituitary function when deficits may be permanent
management: Replace deficient hormones, giving glucocorticoids first to avoid adrenal crisis, then thyroid hormone, sex steroids and growth hormone as needed
Desmopressin for cranial diabetes insipidus arising from posterior lobe or stalk involvement
High-dose glucocorticoids to reduce inflammatory gland enlargement causing headache or visual compromise
Withhold the triggering checkpoint inhibitor and manage jointly with oncology when therapy-induced
Reserve trans-sphenoidal surgery for significant mass effect or diagnostic uncertainty rather than as routine treatment
Serial pituitary hormone testing and interval MRI to monitor recovery, relapse or gland atrophy
Counsel on likely lifelong corticotroph replacement and sick-day steroid rules given frequent irreversibility
